title: Digestive Biochemistry and Dietary Requirements
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers what the body must obtain from food and what happens when intake, absorption, or storage fails. It begins with essential amino acids, essential fatty acids, and the two forms of severe undernutrition, then follows the fat-soluble vitamins, vitamin B12, the water-soluble cofactor vitamins, and the minerals iron, zinc, and copper, and closes with vitamin A and D toxicity. A section on fed and fasting metabolism explains how the liver keeps fuel flowing between meals. Board questions usually describe a deficiency picture and ask for the missing nutrient, the enzyme it serves, or the laboratory value that separates two look-alikes. Linking each finding to the enzyme or protein that fails is the skill that answers them.
prerequisites: Glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation
Lipid digestion: pancreatic lipase, bile salt micelles, and chylomicrons (GI-6, GI-7)
Gastric parietal cell secretion and pancreatic exocrine enzymes (GI-6)
Insulin and glucagon signaling through receptor tyrosine kinase and cAMP pathways
Collagen structure and the steps of collagen synthesis

connections.how: Micelle formation and chylomicron assembly are the steps that, when lost, take vitamins A, D, E, and K down together.
The liver stores vitamins A and B12, makes albumin, clotting factors, and transport proteins, and runs gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis.
Celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, and ileal disease produce the nutrient deficiencies explained here.
Iron, copper, B6, B12, and folate deficiencies are the major nutritional causes of microcytic, sideroblastic, and megaloblastic anemia.
Thiamine, B12, vitamin E, and copper deficiencies damage the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves through defined enzyme failures.

Severe malnutrition from inadequate protein relative to energy, marked by edema, fatty liver, and skin and hair changes.
Severe malnutrition from inadequate total energy, marked by wasting of muscle and fat without edema.
A small aggregate of bile salts, fatty acids, and monoglycerides that carries lipids and fat-soluble vitamins to the enterocyte surface.
A glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells that binds vitamin B12 and allows its uptake in the terminal ileum.

Acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, water-soluble fuels made from fatty acid-derived acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria.

sections.title: Essential amino acids, essential fatty acids, and protein-energy malnutrition

blocks.text: An amino acid is essential when humans cannot build its carbon skeleton at all, or not fast enough to meet need. Nine are essential in adults: phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, leucine, and lysine. Others are conditionally essential. Tyrosine is made from phenylalanine, so it becomes essential in phenylketonuria; cysteine needs sulfur from methionine; and arginine synthesis may not keep up with need during growth or severe stress. Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic, so their carbon skeletons cannot be used to make glucose during a fast.

Humans can desaturate fatty acids only up to carbon 9 from the carboxyl end and lack the enzymes that insert double bonds nearer the methyl end. They therefore cannot make linoleic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid, 18 carbons, two double bonds) or alpha-linolenic acid (an omega-3 fatty acid, 18 carbons, three double bonds), and both must come from food. Linoleic acid is elongated and desaturated to arachidonic acid, the precursor of prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes, and it is a component of the ceramides that seal the epidermal water barrier. Alpha-linolenic acid is converted, inefficiently, to eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acids, which are concentrated in retina and brain. Deficiency, seen with long-term fat-free parenteral feeding or severe fat malabsorption, causes scaly dermatitis, hair loss, and poor wound healing.

blocks.text: Kwashiorkor and marasmus

Protein-energy malnutrition has two classic poles. In marasmus, total energy intake is too low. The body adapts by burning fat and then muscle, so the child is severely wasted, but the amino acids released from muscle keep hepatic protein synthesis going, serum albumin stays near normal, and there is no edema. In kwashiorkor, energy intake may be adequate but protein is insufficient, often after weaning onto a starchy diet or during an infection. The liver lacks amino acids to make albumin and apolipoprotein B-100. Low albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid leaves capillaries as pitting edema and ascites. Without enough apolipoprotein B-100, triglyceride cannot be packaged into VLDL, so it accumulates in hepatocytes as fatty liver.

blocks.text: Children with either form have impaired cell-mediated immunity, thymic atrophy, and frequent infections, and many have mixed features. Oxidative stress and infection may also contribute to kwashiorkor, but the protein-albumin-edema mechanism remains the standard explanation.

sections.title: Fat malabsorption and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K

blocks.text: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are hydrophobic, so they travel the same route as dietary fat. Pancreatic lipase and colipase digest triglyceride, bile salts gather the products and the vitamins into micelles, the micelles deliver them to the jejunal enterocyte, and the enterocyte packages them into chylomicrons that enter lymph. A defect at any step lowers all four vitamins together, along with steatorrhea (bulky, pale, foul-smelling stool with excess fat).

blocks.title: Three routes to fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
steps: Pancreatic insufficiency: too little lipase to digest triglyceride
Cholestasis: too little bile salt to form micelles
Celiac disease: villous atrophy reduces absorptive surface
Micelle uptake or chylomicron formation fails
Steatorrhea with low vitamins A, D, E, and K
blocks.caption: Different lesions converge on the same outcome because all four vitamins depend on intact fat absorption.

blocks.text: Vitamin A (retinol) is converted to 11-cis-retinal, the chromophore of rhodopsin in rods, and to retinoic acid, which binds nuclear receptors that maintain specialized epithelia. Rods fail first because they work in dim light, so night blindness is the earliest sign. Loss of retinoic acid signaling causes squamous metaplasia: a dry, keratinized conjunctiva (xerophthalmia), Bitot spots, follicular hyperkeratosis of skin, and weakened epithelial defenses against infection.

Vitamin D is hydroxylated in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and in the kidney to calcitriol, which raises intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. When it is deficient, a slight fall in ionized calcium raises PTH, which restores calcium by resorbing bone and wasting phosphate in urine. The low calcium-phosphate product leaves newly formed osteoid unmineralized: osteomalacia in adults (bone pain, pseudofractures) and rickets in children.

Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that stops chain reactions of lipid peroxidation in membranes rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids. Red cell membranes then break down under oxidant stress (hemolytic anemia), and long sensory axons degenerate, giving dorsal column loss, spinocerebellar ataxia, and peripheral neuropathy. This resembles B12 deficiency but without megaloblastic anemia or raised MMA.

Vitamin K in its reduced form is the cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase in the liver. Uncarboxylated factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S cannot bind Ca2+ and phospholipid, so they are secreted but nonfunctional. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 4 to 6 hours), so the prothrombin time (PT) prolongs before the partial thromboplastin time. Factor V is not vitamin K dependent: it is normal in vitamin K deficiency but low in liver failure, which separates the two causes of a long PT.

sections.title: Vitamin B12 absorption and the distinction from folate deficiency

blocks.text: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is made only by microorganisms and reaches humans mainly in animal foods, where it is bound to protein. Its absorption requires a relay of binding proteins, each made in a different organ, and failure at any step causes deficiency. Body stores of about 2 to 5 mg, mostly in the liver, cover several years of loss, so deficiency appears long after absorption fails.

blocks.title: Vitamin B12 from food to tissue
steps: Gastric acid and pepsin release B12 from food protein
Free B12 binds haptocorrin (R binder) from saliva and stomach
In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases digest haptocorrin
Released B12 binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells
Cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum take up IF-B12
Transcobalamin II carries B12 in plasma to tissues and liver
blocks.caption: Each step depends on a different organ: stomach, pancreas, and terminal ileum.

blocks.text: Haptocorrin protects B12 in the acid stomach, where B12 binds it more avidly than intrinsic factor; only after trypsin and other pancreatic proteases degrade haptocorrin in the alkaline duodenum can intrinsic factor take over. This is why pancreatic insufficiency can lower B12 absorption even though the stomach is normal.

blocks.title: Where B12 absorption fails
rows: Atrophic gastritis, gastrectomy, long-term acid suppression
Pernicious anemia (autoantibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor), gastrectomy

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum)
blocks.caption: Locating the failed step guides the search for the underlying disease.

blocks.text: Two enzymes, two metabolites

B12 serves only two human enzymes. Methionine synthase, in the cytoplasm, uses methylcobalamin to move a methyl group from N5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, forming methionine and regenerating tetrahydrofolate (THF). Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, in mitochondria, uses adenosylcobalamin to convert methylmalonyl-CoA, derived from odd-chain fatty acids and some amino acids, to succinyl-CoA.

Folate is needed only for the first reaction. A lack of either vitamin therefore raises homocysteine, but only B12 lack raises MMA. In B12 deficiency, folate also becomes trapped as N5-methyl-THF, which cannot be converted back to other forms (the methyl-folate trap). Both deficiencies therefore starve thymidylate synthesis, slowing DNA replication while RNA and cytoplasm keep growing, which produces megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. B12 deficiency alone causes subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts and peripheral neuropathy, attributed to impaired myelin methylation and abnormal fatty acids built from excess methylmalonyl-CoA. Folate stores last only months, so folate deficiency appears sooner, in alcohol use disorder, pregnancy, and poor diets.

blocks.title: Laboratory distinction of B12 and folate deficiency
blocks.caption: MMA is the deciding test because only B12 serves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading homocysteine and MMA
blocks.text: A 62-year-old with macrocytic anemia has a borderline serum B12, high homocysteine, and high MMA. Step 1: high homocysteine means methionine synthase is failing, which fits B12 or folate deficiency. Step 2: high MMA means methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is also failing, and only B12 serves that enzyme. Step 3: conclude B12 deficiency; the metabolites show intracellular function better than the serum level. With normal MMA, folate deficiency would be the answer. Kidney failure raises both metabolites, so renal function must be known first.

blocks.predict: B12 and folate deficiency both cause megaloblastic anemia. Why does only B12 deficiency damage the spinal cord?
blocks.explain: Both vitamins are needed for methionine synthase and thymidylate supply, so both impair DNA synthesis. Only B12 serves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and its failure, together with impaired myelin methylation, is linked to demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on the two enzymes and the methyl-folate trap.

sections.title: Thiamine, niacin, pyridoxine, and vitamin C as cofactors

blocks.text: Water-soluble vitamins are stored in small amounts and turned over quickly, so deficiency develops within weeks to months of poor intake or absorption. Each deficiency syndrome follows from the reactions its coenzyme supports: the tissues that depend most on those reactions fail first.

Thiamine (B1) is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the cofactor for oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids by pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, and for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway. Without TPP, pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and the cycle itself slows, so ATP production falls and lactate accumulates. Neurons, which rely on glucose oxidation, are injured first, especially in the mammillary bodies, medial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray, giving Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia). A glucose load in a thiamine-depleted person increases flux toward the blocked enzymes and can precipitate it. Dry beriberi is a symmetric peripheral neuropathy; wet beriberi is high-output heart failure from peripheral vasodilation and impaired myocardial energy production. Alcohol use disorder is the usual setting, because intake, absorption, and storage are all reduced.

Niacin (B3) forms NAD+ and NADP+, which carry electrons in hundreds of redox reactions. Some niacin is made from tryptophan, a pathway that needs B6 and riboflavin. Tissues with high turnover and energy demand fail first, giving pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis on sun-exposed skin (including a collar around the neck), diarrhea, and dementia. Pellagra follows diets based on untreated maize, Hartnup disease (loss of neutral amino acids including tryptophan through a defective intestinal and renal transporter), carcinoid syndrome (tryptophan diverted to serotonin), and isoniazid exposure, which depletes B6 and so blocks niacin synthesis.

Pyridoxine (B6) forms pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the cofactor for transamination, many decarboxylations, and the first step of heme synthesis. Erythroid ALA synthase needs PLP, so heme production falls while iron keeps arriving; iron accumulates in mitochondria around the nucleus, forming ring sideroblasts, and the anemia is microcytic. Glutamate decarboxylase needs PLP to make GABA, so deficiency lowers inhibitory tone and causes seizures, most often in infants. Peripheral neuropathy, glossitis, and cheilosis also occur.

Vitamin C (ascorbate) keeps the iron in prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in the reduced Fe2+ state. These enzymes hydroxylate procollagen in the rough endoplasmic reticulum; hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix by hydrogen bonding, and hydroxylysine allows glycosylation and cross-linking. Without them, collagen is unstable and is degraded or secreted in weak form, so blood vessel walls, gums, and healing wounds fail. Scurvy presents with perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, easy bruising, poor wound healing, and subperiosteal or joint bleeding. Ascorbate also reduces dietary Fe3+ to absorbable Fe2+ and is a cofactor for dopamine beta-hydroxylase.

sections.title: Fuel supply in the fed and fasting states

blocks.text: Blood glucose must stay near about 70 to 100 mg/dL (3.9 to 5.6 mmol/L) between meals because red cells use only glucose and the brain uses mainly glucose. The liver manages this supply, switching between storage and release under the control of the insulin-to-glucagon ratio.

In the fed state, insulin dominates. Hepatocytes take up glucose through GLUT2, trap it with glucokinase, and store it as glycogen. Insulin-activated phosphatases switch on glycogen synthase and raise fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which stimulates glycolysis, so excess carbon becomes fatty acid and leaves the liver as VLDL.

A few hours after a meal, glucagon dominates. It raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the same enzymes in the opposite direction: glycogen phosphorylase is activated, glycogen synthase is inhibited, and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, so gluconeogenesis is favored over glycolysis. The liver has glucose-6-phosphatase and can release free glucose; muscle lacks it, so its larger glycogen store serves only muscle. Liver glycogen is largely exhausted after about 24 hours.

Gluconeogenesis then becomes the main source. It reverses glycolysis using four bypass enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase (biotin dependent, activated by acetyl-CoA), PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose-6-phosphatase. Lactate from red cells and muscle returns to the liver and is converted to glucose (Cori cycle). Alanine from muscle protein breakdown is transaminated to pyruvate, and its nitrogen goes to urea (glucose-alanine cycle). Glycerol from adipose lipolysis enters as dihydroxyacetone phosphate. Even-chain fatty acids cannot supply net glucose, because pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible and the TCA cycle releases two carbons as CO2 for each acetyl-CoA that enters; only the propionyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids is glucogenic.

blocks.text: Ketogenesis and why the liver cannot use ketones

With low insulin, falling malonyl-CoA releases carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, so fatty acids from adipose lipolysis enter liver mitochondria for beta-oxidation. Because oxaloacetate is drawn off for gluconeogenesis, the acetyl-CoA cannot all enter the TCA cycle and is converted by mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase (rate limiting) to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. Extrahepatic tissues reactivate acetoacetate with succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (thiophorase). The liver lacks this enzyme, so its ketones are exported rather than burned, and red cells, lacking mitochondria, cannot use them. After a week or more, ketones supply up to about two thirds of the brain's energy, lowering its glucose need and so the muscle protein broken down to make glucose.

steps: Low insulin and high glucagon activate adipose lipolysis

HMG-CoA synthase forms acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate
Liver lacks thiophorase, so ketones enter the blood
Brain, heart, and muscle convert ketones back to acetyl-CoA
blocks.caption: Ketogenesis exports fat-derived fuel from the liver to tissues that cannot use fatty acids directly.

blocks.title: Worked example: why fat cannot make glucose
blocks.text: Why does muscle protein break down during a five-day fast when fat stores are large? Step 1: red cells and brain still need glucose. Step 2: acetyl-CoA from fatty acids joins oxaloacetate, and two carbons leave as CO2 before oxaloacetate is regenerated, so no net oxaloacetate or glucose is gained. Step 3: only glycerol, a small part of each triglyceride, is glucogenic. Step 4: the rest must come from amino acids such as alanine, until ketones lower the brain's glucose need. Fatty acid oxidation still helps by supplying the ATP that gluconeogenesis consumes and the acetyl-CoA that activates pyruvate carboxylase.

Iron, zinc, and copper are absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal small intestine, so they share risk from celiac disease, gastric surgery, and bypass of the proximal bowel. They also interact: copper enzymes are needed to move iron, and zinc can block copper absorption.

Dietary nonheme iron is reduced from Fe3+ to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome b on the brush border, a step helped by gastric acid and ascorbate, and enters the enterocyte through divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1). Heme iron is absorbed separately and more efficiently. Iron leaves the cell through ferroportin, is oxidized to Fe3+ by the copper-containing ferroxidase hephaestin, and binds transferrin. Hepcidin from the liver degrades ferroportin and so limits absorption. The body has no regulated route for iron excretion, so balance is set at absorption.

In iron deficiency, stores are lost first (low ferritin), then transport iron falls (low serum iron and transferrin saturation, with high total iron-binding capacity because the liver makes more transferrin), and only then does anemia appear. Developing red cells keep dividing until their hemoglobin concentration reaches a threshold, so too little heme produces extra divisions and small, pale (microcytic, hypochromic) cells. In adults, iron deficiency usually reflects chronic blood loss, from menstruation in premenopausal women and most often from the gastrointestinal tract in men and postmenopausal women.

Zinc is a structural or catalytic cofactor for hundreds of enzymes (including alkaline phosphatase, carbonic anhydrase, and matrix metalloproteinases) and for zinc-finger transcription factors. Deficiency therefore strikes rapidly dividing tissues: poor wound healing, dermatitis around the mouth and anus and on the hands and feet (acrodermatitis), alopecia, diarrhea, impaired T cell immunity, dysgeusia, hypogonadism, and growth failure in children. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an inherited defect of the intestinal zinc transporter ZIP4; acquired deficiency follows alcohol use disorder, malabsorption, and diets high in phytate.

Copper is a cofactor for ceruloplasmin and hephaestin (ferroxidases that allow iron export), cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase, and dopamine beta-hydroxylase. Deficiency causes anemia, because iron is trapped in enterocytes and macrophages, and neutropenia. It also causes a myelopathy of the dorsal columns with sensory ataxia that closely mimics B12 subacute combined degeneration, probably from failed mitochondrial and antioxidant copper enzymes. Copper deficiency follows gastric bypass, which removes the proximal absorptive surface, and excess zinc intake.

sections.title: Vitamin A and vitamin D toxicity

blocks.text: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in liver and adipose tissue and are not excreted readily in urine, so excess intake accumulates. Toxicity follows high-dose supplements, retinoid drugs, or, for vitamin A, eating very large amounts of liver.

The liver stores vitamin A as retinyl esters in hepatic stellate (Ito) cells. When intake exceeds storage capacity, the stellate cells become engorged and activated, laying down collagen in the space of Disse; this causes hepatomegaly, perisinusoidal fibrosis, and in severe cases noncirrhotic portal hypertension or cirrhosis. Excess retinoid also raises intracranial pressure, thought to reflect impaired CSF absorption, giving headache, vomiting, papilledema, and in infants a bulging fontanelle (pseudotumor cerebri). Chronic excess also causes dry, peeling skin, alopecia, bone and joint pain, and increased bone resorption with fracture risk and sometimes hypercalcemia. Retinoic acid controls HOX gene expression along the embryonic axis, so excess early in pregnancy disrupts cranial neural crest development: craniofacial and ear malformations, conotruncal heart defects, and central nervous system defects. Isotretinoin, a synthetic retinoid, carries the same teratogenic risk, which illustrates the receptor mechanism.

Vitamin D toxicity comes from very high intake, which raises 25-hydroxyvitamin D. At high concentrations, 25-hydroxyvitamin D is thought to activate the vitamin D receptor directly and to displace calcitriol from vitamin D-binding protein, raising free calcitriol. Intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and osteoclastic bone resorption both rise, producing hypercalcemia and sometimes hyperphosphatemia. The high calcium acts on the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor to suppress PTH, so renal calcium reabsorption falls and filtered calcium spills into urine (hypercalciuria). This causes calcium stones, nephrocalcinosis, and polyuria, because hypercalcemia blunts the collecting duct response to ADH (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus). Hypercalcemia also causes constipation, nausea, confusion, a shortened QT interval, and calcification of soft tissues when the calcium-phosphate product is high.

Laboratory values separate the causes of hypercalcemia. Vitamin D toxicity gives high 25-hydroxyvitamin D and low PTH. Granulomatous diseases such as sarcoidosis also give low PTH, but macrophages convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol without feedback control, so calcitriol is high while 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal. Primary hyperparathyroidism gives high PTH with low phosphate.

blocks.title: Worked example: a hypercalcemic patient with low PTH
blocks.text: A 48-year-old taking high-dose supplements has serum calcium 12.8 mg/dL (reference about 8.5 to 10.5), low PTH, and kidney stones. Step 1: low PTH means the parathyroids are responding normally, so the calcium source lies elsewhere. Step 2: check vitamin D metabolites. A very high 25-hydroxyvitamin D with only modestly raised calcitriol points to exogenous vitamin D. Step 3: if 25-hydroxyvitamin D were normal and calcitriol high, unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase in granulomas would be more likely. Step 4: stones follow because low PTH and a high filtered load both increase urinary calcium.

integration.text: The deficiencies in this chapter cluster by anatomy. Gastric disease removes acid, pepsin, and intrinsic factor and impairs iron and B12 absorption; pancreatic and biliary disease remove lipase and bile salts and take down vitamins A, D, E, and K; duodenal and proximal jejunal disease or bypass lowers iron, zinc, copper, and folate; and terminal ileal disease removes B12 and bile salt recycling. Reading a patient's surgical history or gut disease therefore predicts which nutrients will run short. Biochemistry then explains the findings: each vitamin or mineral serves specific enzymes, and the tissues most dependent on those enzymes fail first.

Several deficiencies imitate one another, and metabolites or companion tests separate them. B12, copper, and vitamin E deficiency all damage the dorsal columns, but only B12 raises MMA and only copper lowers ceruloplasmin; iron and B6 deficiency both produce microcytosis, but only B6 deficiency leaves iron stores full with ring sideroblasts. Serum levels of vitamins and minerals can mislead, because ferritin and zinc shift with inflammation and serum B12 may stay borderline, so functional markers and the whole clinical pattern carry more weight than any single value.

summary: Essential nutrients are those whose synthesis humans lack: nine amino acids and the omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.
Kwashiorkor is protein lack with low albumin (edema) and failed apolipoprotein B-100 export (fatty liver); marasmus is energy lack with wasting and no edema.
Fat malabsorption from pancreatic, biliary, or mucosal disease lowers vitamins A, D, E, and K together: night blindness, osteomalacia, hemolysis with neuropathy, and a prolonged PT.
B12 absorption needs acid and pepsin, haptocorrin, pancreatic proteases, intrinsic factor, and the terminal ileum; homocysteine rises in B12 or folate deficiency, MMA only in B12 deficiency.
Thiamine (TPP) serves alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenases, niacin forms NAD+, B6 (PLP) serves ALA synthase and GABA synthesis, and vitamin C keeps collagen hydroxylases active.
Glycogenolysis supports glucose for about a day, then gluconeogenesis from lactate, alanine, and glycerol; even-chain fatty acids cannot make net glucose.
The liver makes ketones from fatty acid acetyl-CoA but lacks thiophorase, so it exports them to brain, heart, and muscle.

Iron deficiency gives microcytic anemia with low ferritin and high TIBC; zinc deficiency gives poor healing, dysgeusia, and acrodermatitis; copper deficiency gives anemia, neutropenia, and myelopathy.
Excess zinc induces metallothionein that traps copper; gastric bypass removes the proximal surface that absorbs iron and copper.
Vitamin A excess causes intracranial hypertension, stellate cell liver injury, and birth defects; vitamin D excess causes hypercalcemia with low PTH, hypercalciuria, and stones.

verify: Histidine is listed as essential in adults per current consensus; some older texts list it as essential only in children, and arginine is treated variably as conditionally essential. Confirm the list NABNE expects.
The time to near exhaustion of liver glycogen is quoted from about 12 to 48 hours in different sources; this chapter uses about 24 hours.
Factor VII half-life is quoted from about 4 to 6 hours; B12 body stores of about 2 to 5 mg and folate stores of about 3 to 4 months are common textbook approximations.

Reference ranges for homocysteine, MMA, serum B12, ferritin, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D vary between laboratories; this chapter gives none for metabolites deliberately. Confirm whether NABNE expects specific cutoffs.
The role of oxidative stress and infection in kwashiorkor is an area of ongoing research; the protein-albumin mechanism is presented as the standard explanation.
The mechanisms of copper deficiency neutropenia and myelopathy and of vitamin A-related intracranial hypertension are not fully established; they are described here with hedged wording.
Confirm whether NABNE expects eponyms such as Bitot spots, Casal necklace, Cori cycle, and Ito cells, or only descriptive terms.

No listed diagram fits this chapter. Requested new diagram names for a future revision: b12-absorption (stomach, duodenum, and ileum with binding proteins) and fasting-fuel-timeline (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and ketone use over days).
